claim: Piezo1 and Piezo2 belong to a family of mechanically-activated ion channels implicated in a wide range of physiological processes.
source: Piezo1 and Piezo2 belong to a family of mechanically-activated ion channels implicated in a wide range of physiological processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing the role of Piezo channels in physiology.

claim: Mechanical stimulation triggers Piezo channels to open, but their characteristic fast inactivation process results in rapid closure.
source: Mechanical stimulation triggers Piezo channels to open, but their characteristic fast inactivation process results in rapid closure.
evidence: This is a well-established functional property of Piezo channels supported by the literature.

claim: Several disease-causing mutations in Piezo1 alter the rate of inactivation.
source: Several disease-causing mutations in Piezo1 alter the rate of inactivation, highlighting the importance of inactivation to the normal function of this channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to disease-linked mutations in the introduction.

claim: The mechanism of inactivation in Piezo channels remains unknown despite structural identification of two physical constrictions within the closed pore.
source: However, despite the structural identification of two physical constrictions within the closed pore, the mechanism of inactivation remains unknown.
evidence: This statement sets up the research question and is supported by the lack of mechanistic understanding in prior literature.

claim: A functionally conserved inactivation gate exists in the pore-lining inner helix of mouse Piezo1 and Piezo2 that is distinct from the two constrictions.
source: Here we identify a functionally conserved inactivation gate in the pore-lining inner helix of mouse Piezo1 and Piezo2 that is distinct from the two constrictions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the results.

claim: The inactivation gate in the inner helix controls the majority of Piezo1 inactivation via a hydrophobic mechanism.
source: We show that this gate controls the majority of Piezo1 inactivation via a hydrophobic mechanism and that one of the physical constrictions acts as a secondary gate.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by mutagenesis data showing correlation between hydrophobicity and inactivation rate.

claim: One of the physical constrictions acts as a secondary gate in Piezo1 inactivation.
source: We show that this gate controls the majority of Piezo1 inactivation via a hydrophobic mechanism and that one of the physical constrictions acts as a secondary gate.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that mutations at the MF constriction have moderate effects on inactivation.

claim: Unlike other rapidly inactivating ion channels, a hydrophobic barrier gives rise to fast inactivation in Piezo channels.
source: Our results suggest that, unlike other rapidly inactivating ion channels, a hydrophobic barrier gives rise to fast inactivation in Piezo channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and comparison with other ion channel mechanisms.

claim: Piezo1 has been implicated in blood pressure regulation, vascular development, arterial remodeling, neural stem cell fate determination and endothelium homeostasis.
source: Piezo1 has been implicated in blood pressure regulation, vascular development, arterial remodeling, neural stem cell fate determination and endothelium homeostasis (Rode et al., 2017; Gudipaty et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2016; Koser et al., 2016; Retailleau et al., 2015; Blumenthal et al., 2014; Pathak et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014a; McHugh et al., 2012; Zeng et al., 2018; Szczot et al., 2017; Del Mármol et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Piezo2 is expressed in somatosensory neurons where it plays a major role in the transduction of gentle and painful touch, proprioception, airway stretch, lung inflation and neuronal migration.
source: Piezo2 is expressed in somatosensory neurons where it plays a major role in the transduction of gentle and painful touch, proprioception, airway stretch, lung inflation and neuronal migration (Nonomura et al., 2017; Woo et al., 2015; Ranade et al., 2014b; Ikeda et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014; Maksimovic et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Malfunctions in Piezo1 or Piezo2 are associated with xerocytosis, arthrogryposis, lymphedema and hyperalgesia.
source: Malfunctions in Piezo1 or Piezo2 are associated with a number of human diseases that involve mechanotransduction, including xerocytosis, arthrogryposis, lymphedema and hyperalgesia (Murthy et al., 2018; Szczot et al., 2018; Haliloglu et al., 2017; Alisch et al., 2017; Fotiou et al., 2015; Cahalan et al., 2015; McMillin et al., 2014; Andolfo et al., 2013; Glogowska et al., 2017; Chesler et al., 2016; Zarychanski et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to clinical and genetic studies.

claim: Mechanical stimulation of Piezo channels gives rise to a mechanically-activated (MA) current, which quickly decays due to fast inactivation.
source: Mechanical stimulation of Piezo channels gives rise to a mechanically-activated (MA) current, which quickly decays due to fast inactivation (Lewis et al., 2017; Gottlieb et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: Disease-linked mutations in Piezo1 and Piezo2 specifically affect the inactivation process.
source: Disease-linked mutations in Piezo1 and Piezo2 specifically affect this inactivation process, suggesting that the normal timing of MA current decay is important for animal physiology (Wu et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on disease mutations.

claim: A prolongation of Piezo2 inactivation in somatosensory neurons of tactile-specialist birds suggests that inactivation is involved in the modulation of complex behaviors.
source: In addition, a prolongation of Piezo2 inactivation in somatosensory neurons of tactile-specialist birds suggests that inactivation is involved in the modulation of complex behaviors (Schneider et al., 2017; Anderson et al., 2017; Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative studies in birds.

claim: Inactivation is significantly affected by the known modulators of Piezo1: Yoda1 and Jedi1/2.
source: Inactivation is significantly affected by the known modulators of Piezo1: Yoda1 and Jedi1/2 (Lacroix et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Evans et al., 2018; Syeda et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to pharmacological studies.

claim: Functional Piezo channels are homo-trimers that adopt a unique propeller-like architecture comprising a central C-terminal ion-conducting pore and three peripheral N-terminal blades.
source: Functional Piezo channels are homo-trimers that adopt a unique propeller-like architecture comprising a central C-terminal ion-conducting pore and three peripheral N-terminal blades (Figure 1A) (Guo and MacKinnon, 2017; Saotome et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to cryo-EM structural studies and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Each blade of Piezo channels is composed of 36 transmembrane (TM) segments.
source: Each blade is composed of 36 transmembrane (TM) segments and is thought to contribute to sensing tension in the membrane (Guo and MacKinnon, 2017; Haselwandter and MacKinnon, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The blade of Piezo channels is thought to contribute to sensing tension in the membrane.
source: Each blade is composed of 36 transmembrane (TM) segments and is thought to contribute to sensing tension in the membrane (Guo and MacKinnon, 2017; Haselwandter and MacKinnon, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on structural analysis and modeling cited in the references.

claim: The pore region of Piezo channels contains an outer pore helix (OH), an inner pore helix (IH), an extracellular cap domain and an intracellular C-terminal domain (CTD).
source: The pore region, which contains an outer pore helix (OH), an inner pore helix (IH), an extracellular cap domain and an intracellular C-terminal domain (CTD), is responsible for ion conduction.
evidence: This claim is based on structural information from cryo-EM studies.

claim: The ion permeation pathway in Piezo channels is lined by the IH within the membrane and is surrounded by the CTD as it continues into the cytoplasm.
source: The ion permeation pathway is lined by the IH within the membrane and is surrounded by the CTD as it continues into the cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is based on structural information from cryo-EM studies.

claim: All three cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of Piezo1 indicate the presence of two physical constrictions in the CTD: one formed by residues M2493/F2494 (MF constriction) and the other by residues P2536/E2537 (PE constriction).
source: All three cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of Piezo1 indicate the presence of two physical constrictions in the CTD: one formed by residues M2493/F2494 (MF constriction) and the other by residues P2536/E2537 (PE constriction) (Figure 1B and C) (Zhao et al., 2018; Saotome et al., 2018; Guo and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three cryo-EM structures and reference to Figure 1B and C.

claim: The MF and PE constrictions in Piezo1 define minimum pore diameters of 6 Å and 4 Å, respectively.
source: These constrictions define minimum pore diameters of 6 Å and 4 Å, respectively, thus the structures are assumed to represent a closed state.
evidence: This claim is based on measurements from cryo-EM structures cited in the text.

claim: The cryo-EM structures of Piezo1 are assumed to represent a closed state based on the constriction dimensions.
source: These constrictions define minimum pore diameters of 6 Å and 4 Å, respectively, thus the structures are assumed to represent a closed state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pore dimensions observed in the structures.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type (WT) mouse Piezo1 in HEK293TΔP1 cells produced robust MA currents with fast inactivation kinetics (time constant of inactivation (τinact) = 11.9 ± 0.6 ms).
source: Overexpression of wild-type (WT) mouse Piezo1 in HEK293TΔP1 cells produced robust MA currents with fast inactivation kinetics (time constant of inactivation (τinact) = 11.9 ± 0.6 ms) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Systematic amino acid substitutions at the M2493/F2494 site to hydrophilic or hydrophobic residues had either no effect on τinact (MF/SS, τinact = 13.3 ± 1.1 ms) or prolonged τinact by 1.6–2.7 fold.
source: Systematic amino acid substitutions at the M2493/F2494 site to hydrophilic or hydrophobic residues had either no effect on τinact (MF/SS, τinact = 13.3 ± 1.1 ms) or prolonged τinact by 1.6–2.7 fold (MF/QQ, NN, TT, GG, AA, VV, LL, II, WW, average τinact = 19.4–31.9 ms) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The MF site only moderately contributes to Piezo1 inactivation.
source: These data reveal that the MF site only moderately contributes to Piezo1 inactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis data showing modest effects on inactivation.

claim: There is no correlation between the rate of Piezo1 inactivation and hydrophobicity at the MF site.
source: Moreover, even though the MF constriction is formed by hydrophobic residues (Figure 1C), we found no correlation between the rate of Piezo1 inactivation and hydrophobicity at this site.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis data showing variable effects independent of hydrophobicity.

claim: Mutating P2536 and E2537 to glycines resulted in substantially reduced peak MA currents with only slightly prolonged inactivation (τinact = 17.6 ± 0.8 ms).
source: Mutating P2536 and E2537 to glycines resulted in substantially reduced peak MA currents with only slightly prolonged inactivation (τinact = 17.6 ± 0.8 ms) (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: The PE constriction is unlikely to be involved in Piezo1 inactivation.
source: These data suggest that the PE constriction is unlikely to be involved in Piezo1 inactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis data showing minimal effect on inactivation.

claim: The PE/GG mutation dramatically accelerated deactivation kinetics of a Piezo1 mutant.
source: Instead, we found that the PE/GG mutation dramatically accelerated deactivation kinetics of a Piezo1 mutant (see below and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The physical constrictions at the MF and PE sites in the CTD are important for channel function, but only moderately affect Piezo1 inactivation.
source: Together, these data show that the physical constructions at the MF and PE sites in the CTD are important for channel function, but only moderately affect Piezo1 inactivation, suggesting that the main inactivation mechanism is located elsewhere in the channel.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis data on both constrictions.

claim: The main inactivation mechanism in Piezo1 is located elsewhere in the channel, not at the MF or PE constrictions.
source: Together, these data show that the physical constructions at the MF and PE sites in the CTD are important for channel function, but only moderately affect Piezo1 inactivation, suggesting that the main inactivation mechanism is located elsewhere in the channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modest effects of mutations at the constrictions.

claim: The middle portion of the inner helix (IH) is lined with pore-facing hydrophobic residues (L2469, I2473, V2476 and F2480).
source: We noticed that the middle portion of IH is lined with pore-facing hydrophobic residues (L2469, I2473, V2476 and F2480), two of which are contained within a cluster of conserved amino acids (2473IVLVV2477, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Two of the pore-facing hydrophobic residues in the inner helix are contained within a cluster of conserved amino acids (2473IVLVV2477).
source: We noticed that the middle portion of IH is lined with pore-facing hydrophobic residues (L2469, I2473, V2476 and F2480), two of which are contained within a cluster of conserved amino acids (2473IVLVV2477, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Serine substitutions at L2475 and V2476, but not at other positions, significantly prolonged inactivation (L2475S, τinact = 62.2 ± 2.1 ms; V2476S, τinact = 46.8 ± 1.7 ms).
source: We found that serine substitutions at L2475 and V2476, but not at other positions, significantly prolonged inactivation (L2475S, τinact = 62.2 ± 2.1 ms; V2476S, τinact = 46.8 ± 1.7 ms) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Combining the L2475S and V2476S mutations had a cumulative effect, resulting in an almost ten-fold increase in τinact (L2475S/V2476S, τinact = 103.3 ± 2.9 ms).
source: Combining the two mutations had a cumulative effect, resulting in an almost ten-fold increase in τinact (L2475S/V2476S, τinact = 103.3 ± 2.9 ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on the double mutant.

claim: The L2475/V2476 (LV) site forms part of the inactivation mechanism of Piezo1.
source: These data indicate that the L2475/V2476 (LV) site forms part of the inactivation mechanism of Piezo1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis data showing specific effects on inactivation.

claim: The LV/SS mutant exhibited a persistent current after removal of the mechanical stimulus.
source: Interestingly, the LV/SS mutant exhibited a persistent current after removal of the mechanical stimulus (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The decay of the persistent current in the LV/SS mutant reflects deactivation of Piezo1.
source: The decay of the persistent current reflects deactivation of Piezo1 (Wu et al., 2016), which can be substantially accelerated by the P2536G/E2537G double mutation in the PE constriction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PE constriction could be involved in Piezo1 deactivation, in contrast to the inner helix LV site, which mediates inactivation.
source: This supports the idea that the PE constriction could be involved in Piezo1 deactivation, in contrast to the inner helix LV site, which mediates inactivation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of mutations on deactivation vs inactivation.

claim: Individual or combined serine substitutions at L2475 and V2476 had no effect on whole-cell MA current amplitude.
source: We found that individual or combined serine substitutions at these sites had no effect on whole-cell MA current amplitude (Figure 2C), apparent threshold of mechanical activation (Figure 2D), MA current rise time (Figure 2E), or rectification and relative ionic selectivity (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-G.

claim: Individual or combined serine substitutions at L2475 and V2476 had no effect on apparent threshold of mechanical activation.
source: We found that individual or combined serine substitutions at these sites had no effect on whole-cell MA current amplitude (Figure 2C), apparent threshold of mechanical activation (Figure 2D), MA current rise time (Figure 2E), or rectification and relative ionic selectivity (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-G.

claim: Individual or combined serine substitutions at L2475 and V2476 had no effect on MA current rise time.
source: We found that individual or combined serine substitutions at these sites had no effect on whole-cell MA current amplitude (Figure 2C), apparent threshold of mechanical activation (Figure 2D), MA current rise time (Figure 2E), or rectification and relative ionic selectivity (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-G.

claim: Individual or combined serine substitutions at L2475 and V2476 had no effect on rectification and relative ionic selectivity.
source: We found that individual or combined serine substitutions at these sites had no effect on whole-cell MA current amplitude (Figure 2C), apparent threshold of mechanical activation (Figure 2D), MA current rise time (Figure 2E), or rectification and relative ionic selectivity (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-G.

claim: The inactivation rate of the L2475S and V2476S mutants slowed with depolarization, similar to WT Piezo1.
source: Similar to WT Piezo1, the inactivation rate of the L2475S and V2476S mutants slowed with depolarization (Figure 2H), demonstrating that the mutations did not affect the voltage dependence of inactivation (Coste et al., 2010; Moroni et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and citations to prior work.

claim: The L2475S and V2476S mutations did not affect the voltage dependence of inactivation.
source: Similar to WT Piezo1, the inactivation rate of the L2475S and V2476S mutants slowed with depolarization (Figure 2H), demonstrating that the mutations did not affect the voltage dependence of inactivation (Coste et al., 2010; Moroni et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the voltage-dependent inactivation data.

claim: The L2475S and V2476S mutations did not affect basal current in the absence of mechanical stimulation.
source: Furthermore, the mutations did not affect basal current in the absence of mechanical stimulation, supporting the conclusion that these amino acids do not contribute to channel activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: L2475 and V2476 do not contribute to channel activation.
source: Furthermore, the mutations did not affect basal current in the absence of mechanical stimulation, supporting the conclusion that these amino acids do not contribute to channel activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of effect on basal current.

claim: Residues L2475 and V2476 are specifically involved in Piezo1 inactivation.
source: Taken together, these results show that residues L2475 and V2476 are specifically involved in Piezo1 inactivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive mutagenesis and functional analysis.

claim: There is a strong correlation between hydrophobicity and the rate of Piezo1 inactivation at both L2475 and V2476 positions.
source: Strikingly, we found a strong correlation between hydrophobicity and the rate of Piezo1 inactivation at both positions.
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mutating L2475 to the highly hydrophilic Q or N led to a substantial ~11 fold increase in τinact (L/Q, τinact = 124.5 ± 4.4 ms; L/N, τinact = 112.7 ± 5.4 ms).
source: Mutating L2475 to the highly hydrophilic Q or N led to a substantial ~11 fold increase in τinact (L/Q, τinact = 124.5 ± 4.4 ms; L/N, τinact = 112.7 ± 5.4 ms) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mutations of L2475 to serine or threonine produced a significant, but moderate increase in τinact (L/S, τinact = 62.2 ± 2.1 ms; L/T, τinact = 25.9 ± 1.8 ms).
source: Mutations to ether serine or threonine produced a significant, but moderate increase (L/S, τinact = 62.2 ± 2.1 ms; L/T, τinact = 25.9 ± 1.8 ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Bulky hydrophobic amino acid substitutions at L2475 led to either similar or faster inactivation compared to WT Piezo1 (L/V, τinact = 2.8 ± 0.3 ms; L/I, τinact = 2.8 ± 0.2 ms; L/F, τinact = 10.2 ± 0.4 ms).
source: Bulky hydrophobic amino acid substitutions, on the other hand, led to either similar or faster inactivation compared to WT Piezo1 (L/V, τinact = 2.8 ± 0.3 ms; L/I, τinact = 2.8 ± 0.2 ms; L/F, τinact = 10.2 ± 0.4 ms) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Small hydrophobic G or A substitutions at L2475 resulted in a smaller increase in τinact compared to the effects of large hydrophilic Q or N substitutions (L/G, τinact = 40.2 ± 1.4 ms; L/A, τinact = 22.1 ± 1.4 ms).
source: The small hydrophobic G or A substitutions at L2475 resulted in a smaller increase in τinact compared to the effects of large hydrophilic Q or N substitutions (L/G, τinact = 40.2 ± 1.4 ms; L/A, τinact = 22.1 ± 1.4 ms), lending support to the idea that hydrophobicity is the main factor determining Piezo1 inactivation at L2475 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Hydrophobicity is the main factor determining Piezo1 inactivation at L2475.
source: The small hydrophobic G or A substitutions at L2475 resulted in a smaller increase in τinact compared to the effects of large hydrophilic Q or N substitutions (L/G, τinact = 40.2 ± 1.4 ms; L/A, τinact = 22.1 ± 1.4 ms), lending support to the idea that hydrophobicity is the main factor determining Piezo1 inactivation at L2475 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the systematic mutagenesis data.

claim: There is a similar correlation between hydrophobicity at the V2476 position and inactivation rate.
source: We also found a similar correlation between hydrophobicity at the V2476 position and inactivation rate (Figure 3B), suggesting that both residues contribute to Piezo1 inactivation via a similar mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both L2475 and V2476 contribute to Piezo1 inactivation via a similar mechanism.
source: We also found a similar correlation between hydrophobicity at the V2476 position and inactivation rate (Figure 3B), suggesting that both residues contribute to Piezo1 inactivation via a similar mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar correlation between hydrophobicity and inactivation at both positions.

claim: The isosteric polar substitutions L2475N and V2476T, which presumably decrease hydrophobicity without affecting the size of the pore, both slowed Piezo1 inactivation.
source: Importantly, the isosteric polar substitutions L2475N and V2476T, which presumably decrease hydrophobicity without affecting the size of the pore, both slowed Piezo1 inactivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on isosteric mutations.

claim: The importance of hydrophobicity, rather than pore size, in determining inactivation at L2475 and V2476 is underscored by isosteric polar substitutions.
source: This underscores the importance of hydrophobicity, rather than pore size, in determining inactivation at these two positions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the isosteric mutation data.

claim: L2475 and V2476 together form a hydrophobic inactivation gate in Piezo1.
source: We therefore propose that L2475 and V2476 together form a hydrophobic inactivation gate in Piezo1.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the mutagenesis data showing hydrophobicity-dependent inactivation.

claim: The LV/QQ double mutant exhibited only a marginal prolongation of inactivation compared to the single substitutions (Iremaining/Ipeak at 300 ms, mean ± SEM: WT, 0.0058 ± 0.0007; L2475Q, 0.41 ± 0.03; V2476Q, 0.19 ± 0.03; LV/QQ, 0.49 ± 0.03).
source: We found that the LV/QQ double mutant exhibited only a marginal prolongation of inactivation compared to the single substitutions (Iremaining/Ipeak at 300 ms, mean ± SEM: WT, 0.0058 ± 0.0007; L2475Q, 0.41 ± 0.03; V2476Q, 0.19 ± 0.03; LV/QQ, 0.49 ± 0.03) (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Even though the majority of inactivation was eliminated in the LV/QQ mutant, the channel still exhibited some current decay, suggesting that another gate contributes to inactivation.
source: Thus, even though the majority of inactivation was eliminated in the LV/QQ mutant, the channel still exhibited some current decay, suggesting that another gate contributes to inactivation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the incomplete elimination of inactivation in the LV/QQ mutant.

claim: The quadruple mutant LV/QQ-MF/QQ showed a complete loss of inactivation (Iremaining/Ipeak = 0.89 ± 0.03 at 300 ms).
source: Strikingly, the resultant quadruple mutant (LV/QQ-MF/QQ) showed a complete loss of inactivation (Iremaining/Ipeak = 0.89 ± 0.03 at 300 ms) (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Complete elimination of inactivation in Piezo1 was consistently observed by high speed pressure clamp in the cell-attached configuration.
source: We also consistently observed complete elimination of inactivation in Piezo1 by high speed pressure clamp in the cell-attached configuration, demonstrating that this result is independent of the method of mechanical stimulation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C using an alternative stimulation method.

claim: The MF constriction in the CTD could act in concert with the inner helix hydrophobic LV gate to produce fast inactivation of Piezo1.
source: Thus, our data suggest that the MF constriction in the CTD could act in concert with the inner helix hydrophobic LV gate to produce fast inactivation of Piezo1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the complete elimination of inactivation in the quadruple mutant.

claim: The two putative inactivation gates (LV and MF) are sufficient to account for the inactivation of Piezo1 during mechanical stimulation.
source: Collectively, these data reveal that the two putative inactivation gates are sufficient to account for the inactivation of Piezo1 during mechanical stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the complete elimination of inactivation when both gates are mutated.

claim: The L2475 and V2476 residues are conserved in the Piezo1 homologue, Piezo2 (L2750 and V2751, respectively).
source: The L2475 and V2476 residues are conserved in the Piezo1 homologue, Piezo2 (L2750 and V2751, respectively) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Substituting L2750 or V2751 with hydrophilic serine significantly prolonged inactivation in Piezo2 (WT, τinact = 2.5 ± 0.1 ms; L2750S, τinact = 8.3 ± 0.5 ms; V2751A, τinact = 14.2 ± 1.4 ms).
source: Substituting L2750 or V2751 with hydrophilic serine significantly prolonged inactivation (WT, τinact = 2.5 ± 0.1 ms; L2750S, τinact = 8.3 ± 0.5 ms; V2751A, τinact = 14.2 ± 1.4 ms) (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The double mutants LV/SS and LV/QQ in Piezo2 did not result in functional channels.
source: The double mutants LV/SS and LV/QQ did not result in functional channels.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental attempts to create double mutants in Piezo2.

claim: The effects of serine substitutions at L2750 and V2751 in Piezo2 were specific to inactivation and did not affect whole-cell MA current amplitude, apparent activation threshold, current rise time, relative ion permeability, or voltage dependence of inactivation.
source: The effects of these serine substations were specific to inactivation and did not affect whole-cell MA current amplitude (Figure 5D), apparent activation threshold (Figure 5E), current rise time (Figure 5F), relative ion permeability (Figure 5G–I), or voltage dependence of inactivation (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-J.

claim: The LV site in Piezo2 is specifically involved in inactivation.
source: These data suggest that the LV site in Piezo2 is specifically involved in inactivation, and that the putative inactivation gate in the inner helix is functionally conserved among Piezo channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis data in Piezo2.

claim: The putative inactivation gate in the inner helix is functionally conserved among Piezo channels.
source: These data suggest that the LV site in Piezo2 is specifically involved in inactivation, and that the putative inactivation gate in the inner helix is functionally conserved among Piezo channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the similar effects of mutations in both Piezo1 and Piezo2.

claim: Substituting M2767 and F2768 (homologous to M2493 and F2494 in Piezo1) with glutamines did not affect inactivation in Piezo2 (MF/QQ, τinact = 2.7 ± 0.2 ms).
source: In contrast to Piezo1, substituting M2767 and F2768 (homologous to M2493 and F2494 in Piezo1) with glutamines did not affect inactivation (MF/QQ, τinact = 2.7 ± 0.2 ms) (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Even though Piezo1 and Piezo2 share common elements of inactivation, their mechanisms are not identical and involve components specific to each channel.
source: These results show that, even though Piezo1 and Piezo2 share common elements of inactivation, their mechanisms are not identical and involve components specific to each channel.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of MF mutations in Piezo1 vs Piezo2.

claim: Two conserved hydrophobic residues in the inner helix (L2475 and V2476) are the major determinants of inactivation in Piezo1.
source: We set out to investigate the molecular basis of Piezo channel inactivation and identified two conserved hydrophobic residues in the inner helix (L2475 and V2476) as the major determinants of inactivation in Piezo1.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by the mutagenesis data.

claim: Mutation of the MF constriction formed by residues M2493 and F2494 in the CTD abolishes all remaining inactivation in LV mutants.
source: We also found that mutation of a physical constriction in the cytoplasmic end of the pore – the MF constriction formed by residues M2493 and F2494 in the CTD (Zhao et al., 2018; Saotome et al., 2018; Guo and MacKinnon, 2017) – abolishes all remaining inactivation in LV mutants.
evidence: This is a summary of the finding from the quadruple mutant experiments.

claim: The two residues at the LV site form a hydrophobic inactivation gate, which contributes to the majority of MA current decay (primary inactivation gate).
source: Collectively, our data lead us to conclude that the two residues at the LV site form a hydrophobic inactivation gate, which contributes to the majority of MA current decay (primary inactivation gate), and that the MF constriction acts as a secondary inactivation gate in Piezo1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive mutagenesis data.

claim: The MF constriction acts as a secondary inactivation gate in Piezo1.
source: Collectively, our data lead us to conclude that the two residues at the LV site form a hydrophobic inactivation gate, which contributes to the majority of MA current decay (primary inactivation gate), and that the MF constriction acts as a secondary inactivation gate in Piezo1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the moderate effects of MF mutations and complete elimination of inactivation in the quadruple mutant.

claim: To form a hydrophobic inactivation gate, both L2475 and V2476 residues would have to face the pore in the inactivated state.
source: To form a hydrophobic inactivation gate, both L2475 and V2476 residues would have to face the pore in the inactivated state.
evidence: This is a logical requirement for the proposed hydrophobic gating mechanism.

claim: The cryo-EM structures of Piezo1 in a closed state reveal that only the V2476 residue faces the pore, and that the L2475 residue points away from the pore.
source: Interestingly, however, the cryo-EM structures of Piezo1 in a closed state (Zhao et al., 2018; Saotome et al., 2018; Guo and MacKinnon, 2017) reveal that only the V2476 residue faces the pore, and that the L2475 residue points away from the pore (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Piezo1 inactivation might involve a twisting motion of the IH to allow both L2475 and V2476 residues to face the ion-conducting pore.
source: We therefore propose that Piezo1 inactivation might involve a twisting motion of the IH to allow both L2475 and V2476 residues to face the ion-conducting pore (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic model based on structural analysis and functional data.

claim: The physical diameter of the closed pore at V2476 is 10 Å.
source: The physical diameter of the closed pore at V2476 is 10 Å.
evidence: This is a measurement from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: For a hydrophobic gate to form an energetic barrier to ionic flow, its pore diameter should be less than 6 Å.
source: For a hydrophobic gate to form an energetic barrier to ionic flow, its pore diameter should be less than 6 Å (Zheng et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on hydrophobic gating.

claim: In addition to the twisting motion, the IH is expected to undergo a motion that leads to pore constriction during inactivation.
source: Thus, in addition to the twisting motion, we also expect the IH to undergo a motion that leads to pore constriction (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the requirement for a smaller pore diameter for hydrophobic gating.

claim: The combined twisting and constricting motions of the IH may allow L2475 and V2476 to close the pore by forming a hydrophobic barrier, rather than by physically occluding the pore.
source: The combined twisting and constricting motions of the IH may allow L2475 and V2476 to close the pore by forming a hydrophobic barrier, rather than by physically occluding the pore, but this hypothetical mechanism remains to be tested by obtaining structures in different conformations.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism that remains to be tested.

claim: Hydrophobic gating was initially proposed after observing unusual liquid-vapor transitions of water molecules within model hydrophobic nanopores during molecular dynamics simulations.
source: Hydrophobic gating was initially proposed after observing unusual liquid-vapor transitions of water molecules within model hydrophobic nanopores during molecular dynamics simulations (Beckstein and Sansom, 2003; Hummer et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior computational studies.

claim: The transient vapor states in hydrophobic nanopores are devoid of water within the pore, causing an energetic barrier to ion permeation.
source: The transient vapor states are devoid of water within the pore, causing an energetic barrier to ion permeation.
evidence: This is an explanation of the hydrophobic gating mechanism from prior work.

claim: A hydrophobic gate stops the flow of ions even when the physical pore size is bigger than that of the ion.
source: Thus, a hydrophobic gate stops the flow of ions even when the physical pore size is bigger than that of the ion (Rao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review on hydrophobic gating.

claim: Evidence has accumulated to suggest that hydrophobic gating is widely present in ion channels.
source: Over the past decade, evidence has accumulated to suggest that hydrophobic gating is widely present in ion channels (Rao et al., 2018; Aryal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to reviews on hydrophobic gating.

claim: In most cases, hydrophobic gates act as activation gates in ion channels.
source: In most cases, hydrophobic gates act as activation gates.
evidence: This is a generalization based on the literature on hydrophobic gating.

claim: A number of TRP channels, including TRPV1, have a gating mechanism similar to that found in voltage-gated potassium channels.
source: For example, even though a number of TRP channels, including TRPV1, have a gating mechanism similar to that found in voltage-gated potassium channels (Salazar et al., 2009), others, such as TRPP3 and TRPP2 contain a hydrophobic activation gate in the cytoplasmic pore-lining S6 helix, which was revealed by both electrophysiological (Zheng et al., 2018b; Zheng et al., 2018a) and structural studies (Cheng, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on TRP channel gating.

claim: TRPP3 and TRPP2 contain a hydrophobic activation gate in the cytoplasmic pore-lining S6 helix.
source: For example, even though a number of TRP channels, including TRPV1, have a gating mechanism similar to that found in voltage-gated potassium channels (Salazar et al., 2009), others, such as TRPP3 and TRPP2 contain a hydrophobic activation gate in the cytoplasmic pore-lining S6 helix, which was revealed by both electrophysiological (Zheng et al., 2018b; Zheng et al., 2018a) and structural studies (Cheng, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electrophysiological and structural studies.

claim: The bacterial mechanosensitive ion channels, MscS and MscL, contain a hydrophobic activation gate.
source: The bacterial mechanosensitive ion channels, MscS and MscL, also contain a hydrophobic activation gate (Beckstein et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on bacterial mechanosensitive channels.

claim: The putative hydrophobic gate in Piezo1 seems to act as a major inactivation gate.
source: Our data suggest that the putative hydrophobic gate in Piezo1 seems to act as a major inactivation gate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that the LV gate controls the majority of inactivation.

claim: Serine mutations at L2475 and V2476 specifically modulate Piezo1 inactivation without affecting other functional properties of the channel, including peak current amplitude and activation threshold.
source: Importantly, serine mutations at L2475 and V2476 specifically modulate Piezo1 inactivation without affecting other functional properties of the channel, including peak current amplitude and activation threshold.
evidence: This is a summary of the functional characterization data.

claim: Activation and inactivation gates are formed by separate structural elements in Piezo1.
source: These results indicate that activation and inactivation gates are formed by separate structural elements in Piezo1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the specific effects of mutations on inactivation without affecting activation.

claim: One or both of the MF and PE constrictions evident in the cryo-EM structures could conceivably contribute to an activation mechanism in Piezo1.
source: One or both of the MF and PE constrictions evident in the cryo-EM structures could conceivably contribute to an activation mechanism, but this remains to be investigated.
evidence: This is speculation about the possible role of the constrictions in activation.

claim: The separation of functional gates in Piezo1 is reminiscent of voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav), in which the activation gate is formed by a transmembrane helix, whereas the inactivation gate is formed by an intracellular III-IV linker known as the inactivation ball.
source: The separation of functional gates in Piezo1 is reminiscent of voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav), in which the activation gate is formed by a transmembrane helix, whereas the inactivation gate is formed by an intracellular III-IV linker known as the inactivation ball.
evidence: This is a comparison to the well-known gating mechanism in Nav channels.

claim: The 'ball-and-chain' inactivation mechanism in Nav channels has been well documented to involve pore block by the inactivation ball.
source: This 'ball-and-chain' inactivation mechanism in Nav channels has been well documented to involve pore block by the inactivation ball (Shen et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2017; McPhee et al., 1994; West et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on Nav channel inactivation.

claim: Inactivation in Piezo1 is predominantly accomplished by pore closure via a hydrophobic gate formed by the pore-lining inner helix.
source: However, our data suggest that inactivation in Piezo1 is predominantly accomplished by pore closure via a hydrophobic gate formed by the pore-lining inner helix (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing hydrophobicity-dependent inactivation.

claim: The proposed inactivation mechanism in Piezo1 is different from that in acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs), in which aspartic acid and glycine residues in a pore-lining helix serve as both an activation and inactivation gate by physically occluding the pore.
source: The proposed inactivation mechanism is also different from that in acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs), in which aspartic acid and glycine residues in a pore-lining helix serve as both an activation and inactivation gate by physically occluding the pore (Yoder et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to the gating mechanism in ASICs supported by citation.

claim: The inactivation rate of Piezo1 channels is voltage modulated.
source: The inactivation rate of Piezo1 channels is voltage modulated (Coste et al., 2010; Moroni et al., 2018) and depends on a single positively charged K2479 residue in the inner helix (Wu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on voltage modulation of Piezo1 inactivation.

claim: The inactivation rate of Piezo1 depends on a single positively charged K2479 residue in the inner helix.
source: The inactivation rate of Piezo1 channels is voltage modulated (Coste et al., 2010; Moroni et al., 2018) and depends on a single positively charged K2479 residue in the inner helix (Wu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The putative hydrophobic inactivation gate (L2475/V2476) is located just one alpha turn upstream from K2479.
source: The putative hydrophobic inactivation gate (L2475/V2476) identified in this study is located just one alpha turn upstream from K2479.
evidence: This is a structural observation based on the positions of these residues in the helix.

claim: The close proximity between the hydrophobic gate and K2479 suggests there may be functional coupling between the voltage-sensing and inactivation processes.
source: The close proximity between these elements suggests there may be functional coupling between the voltage-sensing and inactivation processes, but the exact mechanism remains to be determined.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural proximity of the two elements.

claim: By combining mutations in the putative hydrophobic inactivation gate and the MF constriction in the CTD, complete abolishment of Piezo1 inactivation was achieved.
source: By combining mutations in the putative hydrophobic inactivation gate and the MF constriction in the CTD, we were able to completely abolish Piezo1 inactivation.
evidence: This is a summary of the key experimental finding.

claim: The kinetics of Piezo1 recovery from inactivation strongly suggest the existence of two inactivated states in the channel.
source: Indeed, the kinetics of Piezo1 recovery from inactivation strongly suggest the existence of two inactivated states in the channel (Lewis et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on recovery kinetics.

claim: A complete elimination of Piezo1 inactivation shows that the two gates are sufficient to account for the full inactivation process in Piezo1.
source: A complete elimination of Piezo1 inactivation shows that the two gates are sufficient to account for the full inactivation process in Piezo1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the complete elimination of inactivation in the quadruple mutant.

claim: Having two inactivation gates may provide additional dimensions to the regulation of Piezo1 activity.
source: Having two inactivation gates may provide additional dimensions to the regulation of Piezo1 activity.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of having two gates.

claim: Whereas the inner helix site modulates inactivation in both Piezo1 and Piezo2, mutations at the MF constriction only affect Piezo1.
source: Interestingly, whereas the inner helix site modulates inactivation in both Piezo1 and Piezo2, mutations at the MF constriction only affect Piezo1.
evidence: This is a summary of the comparative findings between Piezo1 and Piezo2.

claim: While Piezo1 and Piezo2 share some gating elements, they may not have identical inactivation mechanisms.
source: Thus, while the two channels share some gating elements, they may not have identical inactivation mechanisms, warranting further studies specifically in Piezo2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of MF mutations in the two channels.

claim: The extracellular cap domain has been shown to be an important modulator of Piezo1 and Piezo2 inactivation.
source: The extracellular cap domain, which is located just above IH, has been shown to be an important modulator of Piezo1 and Piezo2 inactivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Transposition of the cap domain between Piezo1 and Piezo2 changes inactivation kinetics accordingly.
source: Transposition of the cap domain between the two channels changes inactivation kinetics accordingly (Wu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The cap domain could act as a coupling element between force-sensing elements of the channel and the inactivation gate in IH.
source: In the context of our data, it could be that the cap domain acts as a coupling element between force-sensing elements of the channel and the inactivation gate in IH.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of the cap domain based on its known effects on inactivation.

claim: Understanding the interaction between the cap and IH is important, as these domains carry many disease-associated mutations.
source: Understanding the interaction between the cap and IH is important, as these domains carry many disease-associated mutations (Alper, 2017; Wu et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to work on disease mutations.

claim: The LV and MF sites are remarkably conserved among Piezo orthologues.
source: Even though the LV and MF sites are remarkably conserved among Piezo orthologues, the channels can exhibit prolonged inactivation, as reported for Piezo1 in mouse embryonic stem cells (Del Mármol et al., 2018) or Piezo2 in mechanoreceptors from tactile specialist ducks (Schneider et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence conservation analysis and citations to prior work.

claim: Piezo1 in mouse embryonic stem cells can exhibit prolonged inactivation.
source: Even though the LV and MF sites are remarkably conserved among Piezo orthologues, the channels can exhibit prolonged inactivation, as reported for Piezo1 in mouse embryonic stem cells (Del Mármol et al., 2018) or Piezo2 in mechanoreceptors from tactile specialist ducks (Schneider et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Piezo2 in mechanoreceptors from tactile specialist ducks can exhibit prolonged inactivation.
source: Even though the LV and MF sites are remarkably conserved among Piezo orthologues, the channels can exhibit prolonged inactivation, as reported for Piezo1 in mouse embryonic stem cells (Del Mármol et al., 2018) or Piezo2 in mechanoreceptors from tactile specialist ducks (Schneider et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In cases where Piezo channels exhibit prolonged inactivation despite conserved LV and MF sites, the slowing of inactivation is probably dictated by other channel regions, post-translational modifications, interaction with regulatory proteins or lipids.
source: In these cases, the slowing of inactivation is probably dictated by other channel regions, post-translational modifications, interaction with regulatory proteins or lipids, which remain to be determined.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms for modulating inactivation beyond the identified gates.

claim: The three recent cryo-EM structures of Piezo1 are assumed to be in a closed conformation.
source: The three recent cryo-EM structures of Piezo1 are assumed to be in a closed conformation (Zhao et al., 2018; Saotome et al., 2018; Guo and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on the interpretation of the cryo-EM structures cited.

claim: To fully understand the conformational changes associated with Piezo1 inactivation, it will be critical to capture Piezo1 and Piezo2 structures in activated and inactivated states.
source: To fully understand the conformational changes associated with Piezo1 inactivation, it will be critical to capture Piezo1 and Piezo2 structures in activated and inactivated states, which will provide clues for the development of treatments for Piezo-associated human diseases.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: Structures of Piezo1 and Piezo2 in activated and inactivated states will provide clues for the development of treatments for Piezo-associated human diseases.
source: To fully understand the conformational changes associated with Piezo1 inactivation, it will be critical to capture Piezo1 and Piezo2 structures in activated and inactivated states, which will provide clues for the development of treatments for Piezo-associated human diseases.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential translational impact of future structural studies.
